The Traveling Salesman Problem. A classic optimization problem in graph theory and theoretical computer science. Given a set of cities and the distance between each pair, the goal is to find the shortest possible route that visits every city exactly once and returns to the starting city. The decision version of the problem is NP-complete, making it a central benchmark for studying optimization and algorithmic complexity.

Formally, the problem asks for the minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle in a complete weighted graph. The decision version asks whether there is a tour of length at most k, and this version is NP-complete. This means that no polynomial-time algorithm is known to solve it exactly for all inputs.

The Held-Karp algorithm uses dynamic programming and is one of the classic exact methods for solving the traveling salesman problem. It operates in O of two to the power of n times n squared time, which is much faster than brute-force search of O of n factorial but still exponential. For large values of n, even this exponential improvement is insufficient for practical computation.

For metric traveling salesman problem—where distances satisfy the triangle inequality—Christofides' algorithm is a famous approximation algorithm. It guarantees a tour no longer than one point five times the optimal tour length, which is a strong performance guarantee.

The problem is heavily studied in operations research and has practical applications. It arises in logistics, where companies need to route delivery vehicles efficiently. It appears in microchip manufacturing, in DNA sequencing, and in many other fields. The traveling salesman problem is paired alongside the knapsack problem as another iconic NP-complete combinatorial optimization problem. Both are used frequently in teaching the theory of computational complexity. Graph coloring shares similar complexity properties and is often studied alongside the traveling salesman problem in graph optimization.
